n: Who made the oldest tools is not known: Australopithecus afarensis, Kenyanthropus platyops or a species not yet identified.

Stone tools are implements shaped from stone by knapping or grinding; the oldest known, from Lomekwi near Lake Turkana in Kenya, are dated to 3.3 million years ago, about a million years before the genus Homo.
Claims reach back 1.5 to 2 million years, but traces of wood ash from about 1 million years ago are the evidence with the firmest scholarly support.

The control of fire by early humans gave warmth, light, protection from predators and a means of cooking; the earliest known controlled use of fire took place in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, 1.79–1.0 million years ago.
Control of fire by early humans

The earliest evidence is indirect, small stone points from Uzbekistan, Sibudu in South Africa (72,000–60,000 years ago) and elsewhere; the oldest surviving bows, from Holmegaard in Denmark, date from about 9000 BCE.
Archery is the use of bows to shoot arrows in hunting and warfare.
Neanderthals may have burned lignite at Les Canalettes in France about 70,000 years ago.
Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock used as fuel.
Its age, with estimates from 9000 BCE to 44,000 years ago, and whether its marks are mathematical are both debated.
The Ishango bone is an engraved bone tool found at Ishango, near the Semliki River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and believed to be about 20,000 years old.
Fired-clay figurines are older: those of Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic date to 29,000–25,000 BCE.

Pottery is the craft and products of forming vessels and other objects from clay fired at high temperatures; the earliest known pottery vessels, from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, date to 20,000–19,000 years ago.
When the first dome was built is not known; the mammoth-bone dwellings of Mezhirich may be the earliest. Corbelled stone domes appear in the Neolithic Near East.

A dome is an architectural element resembling the hollow upper half of a sphere; the earliest found may be four dwellings of mammoth tusks and bones at Mezhirich in Ukraine, dated between 19,280 and 11,700 BCE.
the Fertile Crescent (goats, pigs, sheep, cattle)

Domestication is a long-term relationship in which one species takes over the control and care of another to obtain resources such as meat, milk or labour; domestication by humans began with the dog at least 15,000 years ago.
How beer was first made is debated; the earliest chemically confirmed barley beer, from Godin Tepe in Iran, is 5,400–5,000 years old.

Beer is one of the oldest human-produced drinks, made by fermenting cereal grains; the earliest archaeological evidence of fermentation is 13,000-year-old residues of a gruel-like beer used by the Natufians for ritual feasting at Raqefet…
Ethiopia, the Sahel and West Africa
Dates for its beginning in West Asia range from about 12,000 to 8000 BCE.

The Neolithic Revolution, or First Agricultural Revolution, was the transition of many human cultures from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement, which began in the Fertile Crescent between 10,000 and 8000 BCE.
A mudbrick is an air-dried, unfired brick of mud mixed with a binder such as straw or rice husks, first known from the dwellings of Jericho, dated to 9000 BCE.

Clay tokens are small shaped pieces of clay that stood for animals and goods, first used to keep records in the ancient Near East around 8000–7500 BCE; the earliest known come from the Zagros region of Iran.
Maize is a cereal crop domesticated in Mesoamerica, the staple of the Aztec and other American civilisations.
Estimates for its domestication in China range from 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.
Rice is a cereal grain cultivated in flooded paddies or dry fields and is a staple food across much of Asia and parts of West Africa.
Lake Titicaca region, Peru and Bolivia
The potato is a starchy tuber native to the Andes of South America, spread worldwide after the Spanish conquest.
Estimates of the earliest trepanation vary from 10,000 to 7,000 years ago.

Trepanning, or trepanation, is a surgical intervention in which a hole is drilled or scraped into the human skull, perhaps the oldest surgical procedure with archaeological evidence; at a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 of 120…
Cotton is a plant fibre spun and woven into textiles, one of the most important traded commodities in history.
Irrigation is the practice of applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, with some of the earliest known use dating to the 6th millennium BCE in Khuzistan, south-west Iran.
Taiwan and Island Southeast Asia (Austronesian sails)
When and where the sail was invented is not known; many date it no earlier than the 5th millennium BCE.

A sail is a tensile structure of fabric or another membrane that uses the wind to propel a craft; sailing boats appear on Cucuteni–Trypillian ceramics from the 6th millennium BCE, and excavations of the Ubaid period in Mesopotamia give…
A copper axe from Prokuplje in Serbia may be older, c. 5500 BCE, and smelting may have begun separately in Asia and in Europe.
Copper smelting is the production of copper from its ores at high temperature; the world's oldest securely dated evidence for it, from c. 5000 BCE, was found at Belovode on Rudnik mountain in Serbia.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and the term is also used loosely for related copper alloys such as brass.
Many scholars credit the Sumerians of Mesopotamia; south-eastern Europe, China and Egypt have also been proposed.

The potter's wheel is a machine for shaping, or throwing, clay into round ceramic ware; the oldest found, from the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in western Ukraine, dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BCE.
Indigo is a blue dye obtained from plants, widely used to colour textiles.
Wheeled vehicles appear almost together in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and Europe in the 4th millennium BCE; whether they spread from the Near East is debated.

A wheel is a rotating component, usually circular, that turns on an axle; the oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement, miniature clay wheels found north of the Black Sea, dates from before 4000 BCE.
H. V. Hilprecht dated the Nippur arch to before 4000 BCE.
An arch is a curved structure spanning an opening, bearing the load above it or serving as decoration, first known in the ancient Near East, where the Nippur arch was built before 3800 BCE.
A Confucian text dates silk to about 2700 BCE; archaeology points to the Yangshao period, 5000–3000 BCE.
Sericulture is the raising of silkworms for the production of raw silk, typically by feeding them on mulberry leaves.
The article notes a contrarian view that the clay tokens were not the precursor of writing, and says the meaning and usage of the tokens are still a matter of debate.
Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets, invented in Mesopotamia in the late fourth millennium BCE.
Whether hieroglyphs arose independently or from Mesopotamian writing is debated; signs from Abydos as early as 3400 BCE question Mesopotamian priority.
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, using pictorial signs for sounds and words.
Outriggers may first have been needed after the crab claw sail appeared, around 1500 BCE.

An outrigger canoe is a boat steadied by one or more side floats, or outriggers, fastened to its hull; such boats were developed by the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the islands of Southeast Asia, and they enabled the Austronesian…
It was used at least as far back as the First Dynasty; the oldest written papyri yet found, the Diary of Merer, date from about 2560 BCE.
Papyrus is a writing material made from the pith of the papyrus plant, which grew abundantly in the Nile valley and delta.
Ox-drawn ards may go back to the 6th millennium BCE in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.

A plough is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing; ploughs were at first powered by people, and the larger ox-drawn ard, or scratch plough, followed the domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps…
Who first made true soap, as distinct from earlier soap-like mixtures, is uncertain; Pliny the Elder called it an invention of the Gauls.

Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, often made by mixing fats or oils with an alkali, used for washing and cleaning; the earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials comes from Mesopotamia, c. 2800 BCE.
Some Egyptologists think the nearby enclosure wall Gisr el-Mudir is older; the credit to Imhotep is that of modern Egyptologists.
The Pyramid of Djoser, or Step Pyramid, is a six-stepped stone pyramid at Saqqara in Egypt, built for the Third Dynasty king Djoser in the 27th century BCE.
The form of the Sumerian device is unknown; the oldest surviving counting board, the Salamis Tablet, dates from about 300 BCE.

An abacus, or counting frame, is a hand-operated calculating tool of beads or counters moved on a board or rods, first known in Sumer, where it appeared between 2700 and 2300 BCE with columns for the orders of magnitude of the base-60…

Otto Neugebauer held that the origins of sexagesimal are not as simple, consistent, or singular in time as they are often portrayed, its use always mixing in a strong undercurrent of decimal notation.
Sexagesimal, or base 60, is a numeral system with sixty as its base, which originated with the Sumerians in the 3rd millennium BCE and passed to the Babylonians.
The earliest glass objects are often counted as faience; true glass appears in the 15th century BCE.
Glassmaking is the craft of producing glass objects.
Other early claims are tentative or disputed, at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey (2200–2000 BCE) and Lejja in Nigeria; the old idea of a Hittite monopoly on iron-working is no longer accepted.
Iron smelting is the extraction of iron from ore by heating it in a furnace.
Earlier claims, at Botai in Kazakhstan (3700–3500 BCE) and on the steppe in the 5th millennium BCE, are debated.

The domestication of the horse turned wild horses into domestic animals; genomic evidence places the source of all modern domestic horses in the Volga–Don region of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in present-day southwestern Russia, around…
The origin of terracing in the Andes is poorly understood.
An andén (plural andenes) is a stair-step terrace dug into a hillside for farming, built by pre-Columbian cultures in the Andes by 2000 BCE.
Early aqueducts were also built in the Indian subcontinent, Greece, the Near East and the Nile valley.
An aqueduct is a channel or structure built to carry water from a source to a city, often across valleys on arches.
When and where it began is not known; the bows in the tomb of Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BCE, are among the earliest dated.
A composite bow is a bow made from layers of wood, horn and sinew glued together, giving great power in a short length suitable for use on horseback.
The earliest traces are at Dholavira, a city of the Indus Valley Civilisation; Ashoka’s inscriptions describe stepwells along the roads, and the first rock-cut ones date from 200–400 CE.
A stepwell, or vav, is a well, cistern or pond reached by a long corridor of steps down to the water, developed in India, where the earliest archaeological evidence is at Dholavira.
Some scholars class the Sintashta vehicles as carts and see the chariot as a Near Eastern invention of the early 2nd millennium BCE.
A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman.
An early date of about 1850 BCE and a late one of about 1550 BCE are debated, which decides whether the alphabet arose in Egypt or in Canaan.

The Proto-Sinaitic script is the earliest known trace of alphabetic writing, found in about 30–40 inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and in two at Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt dated to between 1900 and 1800 BCE.
The Minoans may have pioneered the dye; the Phoenicians of Tyre, after whom it is named, may have used it from about 1570 BCE.
Tyrian purple is a deep purple dye produced from murex sea snails, named after the Phoenician city of Tyre.

The article also gives earlier or vaguer dates, none presented as secure: lunar omens in 'reports from Nineveh and Babylon, circa 2500-670 B.C.', Venus observations that 'probably' go back to the second millennium BC but survive in a 7th-century BC copy (the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa), and the Omen Compendia, composed from the beginning of the second millennium onwards.
Babylonian astronomy refers to the systematic observation and mathematical prediction of celestial phenomena developed in ancient Mesopotamia, flourishing under Chaldean patronage.
The surviving copy may reproduce an older original of the Old Kingdom; the suggestion that Imhotep wrote it is conjecture.

The Edwin Smith Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian medical text and the oldest known surgical treatise on trauma, copied c. 1600 BCE, probably at Thebes, from an original that may date from the Old Kingdom.

Rubber is an elastic material produced from the latex of certain tropical trees, which became an important industrial commodity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with the growth of bicycles, automobiles and electrical…
The first single-tube seed drills may go back to Sumer.
A seed drill is a device that sows seeds by placing them in the soil at a set depth; the Babylonians used primitive seed drills around 1400 BCE.
Its mature form implies earlier development, but no older writing has been found.

The oracle bone script is the oldest attested form of written Chinese, carved mostly on ox shoulder bones and turtle plastrons for the Late Shang royal family from the 13th century BCE; inscriptions of King Wu Ding's reign are radiocarbon…

Distillation is the separation of the substances in a liquid mixture by selective boiling and the condensation of the vapours in a still; Akkadian tablets of c. 1200 BCE describing perfumery show that a primitive form was known to the…
No Phoenician inscription is securely dated before the 10th century BCE.
The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 consonant letters, written from right to left, used in Phoenicia and across the Mediterranean for most of the 1st millennium BCE.
Some sources propose an origin in south-east Arabia, and the dating of the Peruvian puquios is disputed.
A qanat is an underground channel that carries water by gravity from mountain aquifers to lowland fields and settlements.
The oldest substantial inscriptions date from about 740 BCE.
The Greek alphabet is the script of the Greek language, in use since the late 9th or early 8th century BCE (conventionally about 800 BCE), with early samples from at least 775 BCE.
Whether Europe's blast furnaces of the 12th and 13th centuries arose independently or from Chinese knowledge is uncertain.

Cast iron is an iron–carbon alloy with more than 2% carbon, valued for its relatively low melting temperature; the earliest known cast-iron artefacts, from what is now Jiangsu in China, date to the 8th century BCE.
Whether it came from Greece (Corinth, by Thucydides) or Phoenicia (Sidon) is disputed; triremes are first definitely recorded in battle about 525 BCE.

The trireme was an ancient Mediterranean galley driven by three banks of oars with one man to each oar, first referred to at the end of the 8th century BCE; scholars are divided on whether it came from Greece or Phoenicia.
Some trace the crossbow and its name into China from Austroasiatic peoples in the 4th century BCE, but older locks from Zhou tombs contradict this.
A crossbow is a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, shot by a trigger mechanism, allowing troops with limited training to shoot powerful bolts.
Guanzhuang in China is the oldest securely dated minting site, and Aegina has also been proposed for the first coins.

Coinage is the minting of small metal pieces for use as money, first known in the 7th century BCE in China, where a factory at Guanzhuang in Henan made shovel-shaped bronze coins between 640 and 550 BCE, and in Anatolia, where the…
The iron plough, or iron-tipped plough, is a plough whose cutting edge is made of iron, allowing deeper and more efficient tillage.
Its western sections may first have been built by the Assyrian kings.
The Royal Road was an ancient highway of the Achaemenid Empire running about 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations along its length.

The three-field system is a crop rotation in which a field bears one set of crops in the first year, another in the second, and lies fallow in the third; it was first used in China in the Eastern Zhou period.
Its oldest sections were dug by the states of Wu and Yue from 486 BCE; Emperor Yang of Sui joined them into one network in 604–609.
The Grand Canal is a vast system of waterways in China linking the Yangtze region with the north.
The Bible credits King Uzziah of Judah with stone-throwing machines about 750 BCE, but in a much later text.
A catapult is a siege engine that hurls projectiles using tension, torsion or human traction, used before gunpowder artillery.
None of its some 60 texts is proven to be by Hippocrates himself.

The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around 60 early Greek medical works associated with the physician Hippocrates, most written in the last decades of the 5th century BCE and the first half of the 4th; none is proven to be his own.

The article mentions possible earlier traces: perforated gnomons projecting a pinhole image of the sun in the Chinese Zhoubi Suanjing (1046 BC–256 BC, with material added until c. 220 AD), and theories that camera obscura effects inspired Paleolithic cave paintings or played a role in Neolithic structures.

A camera obscura is a dark chamber or box in which light passing through a small hole projects an inverted image of the scene outside onto the opposite surface; one of the earliest known written records of the effect is the Chinese text…
The trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a pivoting arm to hurl heavy projectiles, either by human traction or by a heavy counterweight.
The first watermills have been placed in Persia before 350 BCE and in Byzantium and Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE.

A water wheel is a machine that turns the energy of flowing or falling water into power through a large wheel with blades or buckets on its rim; it first appeared in ancient Egypt in the 4th century BCE, where wheels lifted water for…
Securely proven production sites are later: Sri Lanka in the 6th to 10th centuries CE and southern India from the 16th; the early evidence from Kodumanal is preliminary.

Crucible steel is steel made by melting iron, often with fluxes, in a crucible, which allows precise control of its carbon content; it was first developed in southern India and Sri Lanka by the wootz process, with material as early as 300…
It is largely a compilation of earlier Greek mathematics, and how much of it Euclid wrote himself is debated.
Euclid's Elements is a mathematical treatise in 13 books written about 300 BCE by the Greek mathematician Euclid, the oldest surviving large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.
Pliny the Elder named Sostratus of Cnidus as its architect, but that is disputed.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, or Pharos, was a tower built on the island of Pharos at Alexandria in Egypt under the first Ptolemaic kings and completed around 280 BCE.
Copernicus revived it as predictive astronomy in 1543; whether Aryabhata’s system of 499 was heliocentric is debated.

Heliocentrism is a superseded astronomical model that placed the Sun at the centre of the universe, with the Earth and the planets orbiting it; the first person known to have proposed it was Aristarchus of Samos, c. 270 BCE.
Most scholars derive it from a Semitic script, usually Aramaic; earlier inscribed potsherds from Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu are disputed.

Brahmi is a writing system of ancient India that appeared as a fully developed script in the 3rd century BCE; its earliest securely dated inscriptions are the rock-cut edicts of Ashoka, from 250–232 BCE.
Etruscan mail of the 4th century BCE is older, and the Avesta already mentions mail.
Chain mail is armour made of small interlocking metal rings.
It was long thought that the Maya took writing from the Olmec or Epi-Olmec; murals found in 2005 make an independent invention possible.

Maya script, or Maya glyphs, is the writing system of the Maya civilisation of Mesoamerica, known from inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE at late Preclassic sites such as San Bartolo in Guatemala and Chakjobon in Mexico.
Paper is traditionally credited to the court official Cai Lun in 105 CE, but older paper has been found, so its first date and inventor are unknown.
Papermaking is the craft of producing paper from plant fibres, invented in China.
Its date and place of making are disputed: estimates run from 205 to 87 BCE, and Corinth’s colonies, Pergamon and Rhodes have been proposed.

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, a geared model of the Solar System, built in the 2nd century BCE and recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
Rome (first in the harbours near Baiae)
Some scholars think it was developed a century earlier.
Roman concrete, or opus caementicium, is a building material used in ancient Rome: a hydraulic-setting cement mixed with an aggregate, in widespread use from about 150 BCE.
Tea drinking may be far older, under the Shang and in Yunnan, but early words for it are uncertain, and its discovery by Shennong is legend.
Tea is a beverage made from the leaves of the tea plant, native to southern China.
Its origin is disputed: some date it to about 600 BCE, and its absence from the Mawangdui texts of 198 BCE suggests a later start.

Acupuncture is a practice of traditional Chinese medicine in which thin needles are inserted into the body, believed to have originated in China around 100 BCE, when the Huangdi Neijing first documented a system of diagnosis and treatment…

Glassblowing is the technique of inflating molten glass into a bubble with a blowpipe and shaping it, developed by Phoenician and Syrian craftsmen in the 1st century BCE, in what are now Lebanon and Israel.
The Julian calendar is a solar calendar introduced by Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, with a leap year every four years.
The earliest date is uncertain: Takalik Abaj Stela 2 may be older, and the San Bartolo text of about 300 BCE may be the earliest Long Count notation.
The Mesoamerican Long Count calendar counts the days elapsed since a fixed starting date in 3114 BCE, using units based on twenty.
The article allows that a courier service may have existed for a time under the Roman Republic, but says the clearest reference, by Suetonius, states that Augustus created the system.
The cursus publicus was the state courier and transport service of the Roman Empire, established by Augustus, with relay stations along the main roads.
Vitruvius described aeolipiles earlier, about 30–20 BCE; both drew on the work of Ctesibius.

An aeolipile, or Hero's engine, is a simple bladeless steam turbine, a vessel that spins as steam escapes through bent nozzles, described by Hero of Alexandria in the 1st century CE and usually credited to him.
Whether the Western, Chinese and Indian traditions share an origin is an open question.

Alchemy is a philosophical and protoscientific tradition whose common aims were turning base metals into gold and making an elixir of immortality; in its Western form it is first attested in texts written in Greco-Roman Egypt in the first…
A papyrus codex from Ptolemaic Egypt may be older.
A codex is a book of pages stacked and bound at one edge, the ancestor of the modern book, first described in the 1st century CE, when the Roman poet Martial praised its convenience.
Some count the steering oars of Egypt and Rome as rudders; Joseph Needham held that the sternpost rudder reached Europe from China.
A sternpost rudder is a steering blade hung at the centre of a ship's stern, first known from pottery models of Chinese junks of the 1st century CE, under the Han dynasty.
By stricter definitions, whiteness and translucency, porcelain begins in the late Sui and early Tang; Shang dynasty wares are called proto-porcelain.
Porcelain is a fine, hard, translucent ceramic first developed in China.
An older view gave it an eastern origin, in Arab seafaring.
A lateen is a triangular sail set on a long yard mounted at an angle on the mast and running fore and aft; it originated in the Mediterranean as early as the 2nd century CE, in Roman times.
Its origin is disputed: Kuhn and Cheng argue for China, where dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it; others place it in India, or in the Middle East, where it was known by 1030.

The spinning wheel is a device in which a hand- or foot-turned wheel drives the spindle that spins fibres into thread or yarn; its origin is disputed, and some scholars hold that Chinese dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it.
Galen was a Greek physician of the second century CE whose writings dominated medicine for centuries.
These were prints on silk; the earliest prints on paper date from about 650–670, and the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.
Woodblock printing is a technique of printing text or images by carving them in relief on a wooden block, inking it and pressing paper onto it.
The dating of its oldest witness, the Bakhshali manuscript, is disputed; the first dated, undisputed zero is the Gwalior inscription of 876.
The Hindu–Arabic numeral system is the decimal place-value system of writing numbers with ten digits, including zero, used throughout the world today.
Its date is much debated: its composition may have begun in the last centuries BCE, and proposals range from 2000 BCE to the 6th century CE.
The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on medicine and surgery attributed to Sushruta, one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda.
Toe loops were used in India by the 2nd century BCE, some credit the Sarmatians, and a single iron stirrup from Mongolia is dated 243–405 CE.
A stirrup is a light frame or ring hung by a strap from a saddle to hold a rider's foot, first known in China under the Jin dynasty in the early 4th century CE.
The first modern oil wells were drilled near Baku in 1846–1848.
An oil well is a hole bored into the Earth to bring petroleum to the surface; the earliest known were drilled in China in 347 CE.
Whether Ptolemy or earlier astronomers used it is debated, and its attribution to Hypatia rests on a misreading.

An astrolabe is an astronomical instrument that serves as a star chart and model of the visible sky, used to measure the altitude of stars and find latitude; it dates from classical antiquity, and Theon of Alexandria (c. 335–405) wrote a…
Sugarcane is a tall tropical grass whose stalks are crushed to produce sugar.
The modern cotton gin is credited to Eli Whitney in 1793, though some credit Catharine Littlefield Greene with suggesting its brush.

The cotton gin is a machine that separates cotton fibres from their seeds; the earliest evidence of it is a single-roller gin depicted in 5th-century Buddhist paintings in the Ajanta Caves in western India.
Mesoamerica: south-central Mexico and Central America (earliest at Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas)
Placeholder zeros are older, in Babylonian texts from about 700 BCE, and Ptolemy used a zero by 150 CE; Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in the 7th century.

Zero is the number for an empty quantity and the placeholder digit of positional notation, which in its modern use derives from India, where a Jain text internally dated to 458 CE uses a decimal place-value system including zero.
An earlier, doubtful depiction comes from a 3rd-century tomb in Sichuan, and some see a partial collar in ancient Rome.
A horse collar is a padded harness collar that spreads a load across a horse's shoulders and chest without pressing on its windpipe; it was invented in China by the early medieval period.
No record from the time of its building survives; the credit to Li Chun comes from later chronicles.

The Anji Bridge, or Zhaozhou Bridge, is a stone bridge over the Xiaohe River in Zhao County, Hebei, built in 595–605 under the Sui dynasty and credited to the craftsman Li Chun; it is the world's oldest open-spandrel segmental arch bridge…
Fire-carrying ships may predate Kallinikos’s arrival, and some think it was the work of the chemists of Constantinople rather than one man.
Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire, typically projected from siphons on warships, and able to burn on water.

Maya blue is a turquoise or azure blue pigment made by cultures of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, such as the Maya and Aztecs, from about 800 CE; it combines indigo dye from the leaves of the anil plant with palygorskite, a natural clay.
A possible proto-quipu from Caral, of 3000–1800 BCE, has yet to be evaluated.

A quipu, or khipu, is a record-keeping device of knotted cords of cotton or camelid fibre, first undisputedly attested in the central Andes in the Middle Horizon, c. 600–1000 CE, when it was probably used by the Wari Empire.
Al-Walid I’s foundation at Damascus in 707 may have been a leprosarium rather than a hospital, and Harun al-Rashid’s traditional hospital of 787 is questioned.

A bimaristan is a hospital of the medieval Islamic world; the first true one was probably founded in Baghdad under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, and the first documented general hospital arose there in 805.
Gunpowder is an explosive mixture of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur, first developed in China.
Whether earlier work, from the Rhind papyrus to Diophantus and Brahmagupta, counts as algebra is debated.
Algebra is the branch of mathematics that deals with symbols and the rules for manipulating them to solve equations.
The modern industry began with lamp oil from coal: Abraham Gesner claimed priority from 1846 and James Young patented his process in 1850.

Kerosene, also called paraffin, is a combustible hydrocarbon liquid distilled from petroleum and used as a fuel for lamps, stoves and jet engines; the distilling of crude oil into kerosene was first written about in the 9th century by the…
Whether the vertical windmill of 12th-century Europe owed anything to the Persian one is unclear.
A windmill is a machine driven by wind acting on vanes or sails to grind grain or pump water, first known in Persia, where windmills were working in Khorasan in the 9th century.
The fire lance was an early gunpowder weapon: a tube of gunpowder, usually bamboo, strapped to a spear or other polearm, with the earliest evidence from China in 950.
Diodorus Siculus credits engineers of Ptolemy II with a lock in Egypt about 274 BCE, but not a pound lock.
A pound lock is a chamber with gates at both ends in which the water level is raised or lowered to move boats between levels of a waterway, first built in Song dynasty China by Qiao Weiyue in 984.
The Book of Optics is a seven-volume treatise on optics written between 1011 and 1021 by the medieval Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen (965–c. 1040).
Merchants in Sichuan issued the first notes, the jiaozi; the government took over their production in 1023.
Paper money is currency printed on paper rather than minted in metal.
The Canon of Medicine is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books compiled by Ibn Sina (Avicenna), begun in Gorganj and completed in Hamadan in 1025.
Whether Asian movable type influenced Gutenberg is debated.
Movable type is a printing system using individual, reusable characters that can be arranged to form texts.
A lodestone “south-pointing spoon” for divination is attributed to the Han in the 2nd century BCE, but none has been found.
The magnetic compass is a navigational instrument that uses a magnetised needle to indicate direction.
Culhuacan may have built the first chinampas about 1100; the Aztecs did not invent them but farmed them on a far larger scale.
A chinampa is an artificial agricultural plot built up from mud and vegetation in shallow lake beds, separated by canals.
Where it was first built is not agreed: al-Tarsusi’s description of 1187 implies it was not new, and earlier cases have been argued from sieges between 1090 and 1165.
A counterweight trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a heavy falling weight to swing a throwing arm, capable of hurling large stones over long distances.

A rocket is an elongated flying vehicle driven by a rocket engine, carrying all its propellant and so needing no surrounding air; gunpowder rockets evolved in China under the Song dynasty by the 13th century.
The name covered different hulls over the centuries; the ocean-going caravel of the voyages of exploration was developed in 15th-century Portugal.
A caravel was a small, highly manoeuvrable sailing ship, often with lateen sails that allowed it to sail close to the wind.
Estimates for the first true cannon run from about 1200 to 1280; the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the oldest with a date inscribed.
A cannon is a large-calibre gun, a type of artillery firing a projectile with an explosive propellant, first securely attested in China in the 13th century.
